I maintain a set of REST microservices (Go and Node.js, running in Docker on Linux) and our API regression suite is mostly hand-written Postman collections. Keeping them updated as endpoints change takes too much time, and our mocks for downstream services (Postgres, Redis, a couple of third-party APIs) drift from real behaviour.

I’m looking for a tool that can:

Generate API test cases automatically, ideally by recording real requests/responses rather than me writing each assertion Create mocks/stubs for dependencies (DB calls, external HTTP) from that same recorded traffic Run headless in CI (GitHub Actions) and fail the build on regressions Run on Linux, either open-source or with a usable free tier Ideally not require code changes or SDK instrumentation in every service

What I’ve looked at so far:

I went through this roundup of api automation testing tools to narrow things down. Postman/Newman and REST Assured work, but tests are still written by hand. I’ve also seen Keploy mentioned for record-and-replay testing, but I’d like to hear from people who’ve used it, or alternatives, in a real CI pipeline before committing.

What would you recommend, and how well does it handle noisy fields like timestamps and random IDs in responses?

The program should be something like

run-single-flag-args-file \
  "a-command" \
  "the-single-letter-option" \
  "the-file-with-the-arguments-to-give-to-the-option

The arguments in the file are set each on a line and the whole line is the argument.

Something similar has been asked onto this question on Unix Stack Exchange but it's not specifically for a program, everybody has answered with code rather than with a program and they are gonna delete the answer in which I reply with a program.

Since I would like to find the program which fulfills the request of this question when I look for it, I'm opening it here, where it's appropriate to specifically request a program and people can't complain about the fact they don't like an answer without writing the requested program themselves.
